transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Morgan Lee (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Reliability), Jenna Ortiz (Elysium Head of ML), Marcus Wilde (Elysium Infra), Priya Suri (Elysium PM), Alan Kwok (Elysium SecOps)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy): Discussed autoscaling; target SLOs; need to avoid overprovisioning during Black Friday; recommended reserve + burst pool with token bucket throttling.

[00:00:05] Samir: hey everyone thanks for jumping on, we'll use the first 10 minutes to confirm requirements then deep dive into simulations and policy knobs. Jenna, can you quickly restate peak targets?
[00:00:18] Jenna: yeah so our current p95 target for customer-facing snippets is about 200 to 250 ms, but during promo spikes we see request rates go from ~400 rps to 2k rps in under 3 minutes, which is what's causing cost explosions. We want to keep p95 under 300ms even in bursts, and we prefer not to double our baseline GPU count for the season.
[00:00:40] Marcus: quick correction — our backend also has synchronous downstream calls so end-to-end latency requirement is tighter, we actually can't exceed 350ms total otherwise storefront timeouts.
[00:00:49] Morgan: okay noted. so two engineering constraints: 1) short steep bursts to 2k rps, 2) strict p95 SLO ~300ms. We'll walk through policies that blend reserved capacity + burst credits + queueing with backpressure.
[00:01:10] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[00:01:15] Samir: one high-level architecture we use—reserved GPU pool for baseline concurrency, then a smaller burst pool and a queued overflow path that applies throttling and graceful degradation, plus an async fallback path for non-latency-critical work. Important detail: KV cache warmup reduces per-token compute by ~15-30% depending on model and prompt repetitiveness.
[00:01:40] Jenna: how do you model the queueing? we looked at Erlang-C earlier but wondered if that fits our tail-heavy distribution.
[00:01:48] Morgan: good point. Erlang-C assumes Poisson arrivals with exponential service, which is rough for promo spikes. we try three sims: M/M/c as a baseline, Erlang-C for queued probabilities, and a custom sim that models a token-bucket arrival (bursty arrivals with a hard cap) plus variable service times influenced by KV cache hit/miss. we'll share plots.
[00:02:15] Morgan: for example, with your trace and a 70% KV hit-rate, our sim shows p95 under 280ms with a reserved pool sized for 450 rps and a burst pool that can handle +1.2k rps for up to 6 minutes using token-bucket credits. if KV hit-rate drops to 30% you need roughly 1.8x the baseline GPUs or more aggressive batching which increases latency.
[00:02:40] Marcus: ok but what about cold-starts for new models or after scale-ins? we can't have spikes where first requests are 1.5s and cascade timeouts.
[00:02:50] Morgan: yes, cold-starts are critical. we recommend keeping a small warm pool — N_warm instances pinned per model per region — and an automatic warmup script that pre-warms KV cache by running short prefix batches with representative prompts. That reduces KV miss penalty and model init jitter. the sim includes cold-start penalties as a separate latency component.
[00:03:12] Jenna: can you quantify the warm pool cost vs p95 benefit? we're trying to justify budget to finance.
[00:03:18] Samir: rough numbers from similar customers: a warm pool of 2 GPUs per critical model reduced burst p95 by ~120ms and cut error spikes by 80% during the first 5 minutes. cost is variable — typically 10-15% of baseline reserved spend but offsets queue SLA violations. we'll attach a TCO spreadsheet.
[00:03:38] Priya Suri: what's the recommended autoscale cooldown and scale rate? we saw in-house scaling oscillations before.
[00:03:45] Morgan: set a conservative scale-up fast-path (immediate allocation of burst-prep capacity within 30–60s) but scale-down cooldown longer — 10–20 minutes — to avoid thrash. also smoothing via exponential moving average on request rate helps. policy knobs: min-provision, burst-credit bucket size, max-burst-duration, queue-depth threshold, and fallback model routing.
[00:04:10] Alan: security question — if we warm KV cache with customer prompts, do you persist any PII? how is that handled in Private / VPC setups?
[00:04:18] Samir: good call. for Private deployments we give you the option to disable persistent KV or to encrypt cached entries with your KMS/HSM; warmup jobs can use obfuscated prompts or synthetic traffic derived from traces. we'll also provide the security playbook and the audit log mapping for cache operations.
[00:04:38] Jenna: can we talk about batching and quantization tradeoffs? we run longer completions sometimes and worried about tokenization costs.
[00:04:46] Morgan: batching increases throughput but can increase tail latency for individual short requests if you wait to assemble a batch. our runtime uses dynamic micro-batching — very short batching windows (~20ms) for low-latency tiers and larger windows for bulk workers. Quantization: int8 gives big memory and throughput wins with modest quality drop for many models; int4 is aggressive and can introduce regressions on some NLU cases. recommended approach: baseline in int8 for burst pool, keep highest-quality fp16/int8 mix for reserved latency-critical pool and use eval harness to catch regressions.
[00:05:18] Marcus: If we use quantized variants during bursts, how do you manage model-switching without cache invalidation headaches?
[00:05:26] Morgan: we route requests to compatible variants; prefix/kv caches are keyed by model-variant tags so if you switch variant we either keep separate caches or provide a coherent invalidation. warmup procedures pre-populate both variant caches if you expect to fallback. there's some overhead but it's manageable compared to full cold-starts.
[00:05:45] Speaker 1: (background noise)
[00:05:50] Priya Nair: a note on observability: we recommend token-level cost and latency at route granularity, plus a synthesized "burst diagnostic" dashboard that overlays token/req rates vs p95 and KV hit-rate. this helps tune token-bucket size in real time.
[00:06:10] Jenna: okay can you walk through a real simulation scenario — maybe our Black Friday spike pattern?
[00:06:16] Morgan: sure. we loaded your 30-day trace and fed it into three sims. Variant A: baseline reserved only (no burst credits) — required 4x baseline GPUs to keep p95 under 300ms during spikes. Variant B: reserved + burst tokens (token-bucket with burst credits refill over 30m) + warm pool — required 1.3x baseline reserved + small burst pool to absorb initial surge; p95 stayed ~270ms. Variant C: aggressive batching + heavier quantization for burst pool — lowest cost but p95 at 320–350ms during tail events, which fails your SLO. we flagged tradeoffs in the spreadsheet.
[00:07:00] Marcus: you mentioned a queue overflow path earlier. what's the strategy for requests that cannot be instantly served?
[00:07:07] Morgan: three-tier approach: immediate route to reserved pool (low-latency), then burst pool (medium-latency with possible quantized models), then queued async path which returns a lightweight 202 + notification or degraded response. we also expose per-route queue thresholds and can route non-critical features to the async path automatically during overload.
[00:07:28] Jenna: what about retry storms and client-side backoff? we need client guidance too.
[00:07:33] Samir: provide circuit-breaker guidance: exponential backoff with jitter, and a short TTL cache for recently failed tokens to avoid hammering. Redwood can also emit a 429 with Retry-After and a hint header that indicates remaining burst credit percentage so clients can adapt gracefully.
[00:07:53] Priya Suri: in Private deployments, how flexible is autoscaling? we can't spin up cloud GPUs dynamically in on-prem.
[00:07:59] Morgan: for on-prem / VPC you have two patterns: 1) elastic private in a cloud region with dedicated nodes (we manage autoscale on your VPC subnets), 2) on-prem appliance where autoscaling is constrained — there we rely on smarter policies: larger warm pools, heavier reliance on async fallbacks, pre-scheduled capacity for predictable events, and aggressive quantization/batching. the sim will represent hardware limits.
[00:08:27] Marcus: if we schedule pre-scaling for known promos, can we test it end-to-end? we need a rehearsal run.
[00:08:33] Samir: yes — we suggest a rehearsal where we replay a scaled-down version of your Black Friday trace in a 2-hour window, observe end-to-end latencies, and iterate policies. Morgan will run a pilot test and produce a post-mortem with policy tweaks.
[00:08:49] Alan: from security perspective, we need an attestation that warmup jobs won't leak PII if using real traces, and a map of who can access cache keys.
[00:08:58] Priya Nair: we have role-based controls for cache ops and integration with customer KMS for encryption at rest; we'll include a table in the security doc detailing responsibilities and data flows.
[00:09:12] Samir: quick recap of the recommended starting policy for Elysium: reserved pool sized for median+10% traffic (approx capacity for 450 rps), warm pool of N=2 GPUs per critical model, burst credit bucket sized for 1.2k sustained burst for up to 6 minutes, queue depth threshold at 200 requests with async fallback, scale-down cooldown 15 minutes, dynamic batching windows 20ms for latency tier and 100–200ms for throughput tier, use int8 on burst pool, keep fp16 for reserved. we'll send the exact knobs.
[00:09:50] Jenna: that sounds reasonable. can you quantify expected monthly spend delta vs current plan?
[00:09:57] Samir: we'll have a cost model in the spreadsheet: expected increase ~12% for reserved+warm but total expected savings vs naive 4x overprovision approach is ~40% during peak season. numbers depend on KV hit-rate and quantization fidelity; that's why we need your traces.
[00:10:15] Morgan: one more nuance — if you have multi-region failover, we recommend asymmetric capacity: primary region holds more warm instances, secondary holds smaller warm pool and acts as overflow; routing policies should favor local low-latency variants and use remote as fallback.
[00:10:33] Priya Suri: timeline? when can we get the simulation & runbook?
[00:10:38] Samir: Morgan will run sims and send spreadsheet by 2025-11-12; Samir will send burst policy explainer + runbook by 2025-11-07; security docs and Private deployment checklist by 2025-11-10. we'll aim to schedule pilot baseline week of 11/17.
[00:10:55] Jenna: ok thanks, this was helpful. any final concerns from the team?
[00:11:03] Marcus: just that the sim needs to include our downstream call variance — I'll export traces showing our DB tail latencies and share.
[00:11:10] Alan: and I'll review the KMS integration matrix.
[00:11:14] Samir: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with attachments and calendar invites.

Transcript notes: transcriber occasionally mislabels speakers and drops punctuation. references mentioned: "burst-policy-sim.xlsx" (link via Salesforce), security playbook (redwood/security/burst-warmup.pdf), pilot runbook (redwood/runbooks/autoscale-rehearsal.md).

End of call.
